chief_complaint: pain out of proportion to injury, pain on passive toe stretch
hpi_details: A 74-year-old female presents to the clinic with pain out of proportion to injury, pain on passive toe stretch. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the splint and bandages on her injured leg were wrapped much too tightly and are cutting off all blood circulation.
concerns: She is terrified that the blood supply to her foot has completely stopped and her leg will have to be amputated.
expectations: She hopes the doctor will immediately cut off the tight bandage or splint and give her strong medication to stop the agony.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Compartment Syndrome evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Compartment Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Management requires immediate removal or splitting of constrictive dressings/casts, limb positioning at heart level, and emergent surgical assessment; pressure measurement can support uncertain cases but must not delay fasciotomy when clinical suspicion is high.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: pain out of proportion to injury, pain on passive toe stretch

Key HPI features: A 74-year-old female presents to the clinic with pain out of proportion to injury, pain on passive toe stretch. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Compartment Syndrome.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Compartment Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Simple post-fracture pain without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Pain out of proportion, worse with passive stretch.
management_principles: Immediately remove or split constrictive dressings/casts and position the limb at heart level; obtain emergent surgical assessment and do not delay fasciotomy for pressure measurement when clinical suspicion is high
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: Is the pain much worse than expected?
Does it hurt badly when your toes are moved for you?

history.answer: My injured right leg hurts so terribly bad. The pain has become completely unbearable, much worse than when I first hurt it yesterday.

I tripped over a rug at home yesterday morning and broke my lower right leg, so the clinic put a splint on it. This excruciating deep pressure pain started about six hours ago and has been ramping up ever since.
The pain is deep inside my right calf and shin, feels like my lower leg is about to burst open, and radiates down toward my ankle.
It is a relentless, crushing, burning ache deep inside the muscle. It is definitely a ten out of ten, easily the worst pain I have ever experienced.
The pain is constant without a second of relief, and it has gotten progressively more intense every hour.
Yes, whenever my toes are bent backwards or moved even the slightest bit, the burning agony in my shin shoots through the roof.
Any movement of my foot or touching the front of my leg makes it scream in pain, and having my leg resting flat does not help at all.
Nothing makes it any better. Elevating it actually seemed to make the throbbing ache even more intense.
I took the strong prescription pain pills the clinic gave me for the fracture, but they did not touch the pain at all.
My right toes have started feeling numb and tingly over the last couple of hours, like pins and needles.
It feels very stiff and weak, and I can barely lift my right big toe or bend my foot upward because of the terrible weakness and pain.
My lower leg feels like an overinflated basketball, rock-hard and extremely tight under the splint.
My toes look slightly pale and feel a bit cool compared to my other foot, but they are not blue.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweats.
I feel completely worn out, exhausted, and dizzy from dealing with this nonstop, agonizing pain.
No, I have not had any unintentional weight loss, cough, or night sweats.
No, I have never broken a bone or felt anything remotely like this before in my life.
I tried loosening the outer bandage slightly and resting in bed, but it did not relieve the horrible pressure inside.
I cannot walk, sit comfortably, or sleep at all; the pain is keeping me in pure agony.
I think whoever wrapped my leg put the bandage on way too tight, and it's strangling all the blood flow to my foot.
I'm terrified that the tissue in my leg is dying and you're going to have to amputate it.
I need you to cut this tight wrapping off my leg right this second and give me something strong for the pain.
I have always been healthy with no chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or heart disease.
I have never had any surgeries or previous hospital admissions.
I only took the pain medicine prescribed yesterday for the broken leg, and I take no other regular medications, over-the-counter drugs, or supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only have a small glass of wine once or twice a year during holidays.
I am a retired teacher and I live comfortably at home with my husband.
There is no family history of blood clots, bleeding disorders, or bone diseases.

exam.finding: Alert elderly female in visible acute distress, grimacing and guarding her right lower leg.
Blood pressure 142/86 mmHg, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.8 C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
The right lower leg is extremely tense, tight, and exquisitely tender across all compartments on palpation.
Tight, shiny, and pale skin over the right lower leg beneath the splint, with no redness, warmth, or open wounds.
Passive plantar flexion and stretch of the right toes elicits severe, agonizing pain in the anterior and deep calf compartments.
Weakness with active dorsiflexion of the right ankle and great toe against resistance, limited by severe pain.
Hypoesthesia to light touch and pinprick sensation over the first web space and dorsum of the right foot.
Severe tense, non-yielding swelling of the right lower leg with a firm, woody consistency compared to the normal left leg.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are intact and palpable bilaterally, though slightly diminished on the right; capillary refill is two seconds.
Sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal respiratory excursion and no wheezes or crackles.
